chapter_theme: Under the heading பெரியாரைப் பிழையாமை, five verses on offending the great: belittling them is no wisdom and leaves their standing whole, the insolence of the small is a blind walk to death, the unlearned who needle them hide behind a shrub, a repeated offence is not forgiven, and long association does not save one who strays.

60.reading: To treat the great as small is neither wisdom nor grace nor even sound knowing, and it brings harm on the one who does it; a hall where the assembly once sat stays a hall even if it is cut into.
60.nuance: The verse denies the slight three goods in a row (அறிவு, அழகு, அறிவது) before naming its cost (பாடு). The proverb is hard: on the reading taken here, மன்று is the assembly's hall, and its standing survives damage, so the great keep their greatness even when diminished or slighted. Line 4's என்றூடு is obscure, and the proverb could also mean that a quarrel (ஊடு) broken off still leaves the assembly a place of judgement.

pazhamozhi.literal: the place where the assembly sat is still the assembly hall even if it is cut through

story.act: no story; the proverb's hall stands for anyone whose standing does not end when it is damaged or slighted

pazhamozhi.applied_to: belittling the great does not make them small and only harms the one who belittles

61.reading: For small men to stand before the great, say a scoffing 'is that so?' and keep behaving with insolent boldness of their own accord is like a man with his senses confused, not knowing his way, who walks into a town and does not see the place where he will die.
61.nuance: ஆமாலோ is the small man's mock assent, the tone of the insolence rather than an argument. The verse makes the offender blind rather than wicked: his fault is that he cannot see where he is going. Only the closing quotation mark is printed, so the proverb's start is not fixed; it is taken here as lines 3 and 4.

pazhamozhi.proverb: போமாறு அறியாப் புலன்மயங்கி ஊர்புக்குச் சாமாகண் காணாத வாறு
pazhamozhi.literal: like one who, not knowing the road and with senses dazed, enters a town and does not see where he will die

story.act: no story; a dazed traveller who walks into the place of his death without seeing it

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the insolence of the small toward the great is a blind walk to their own death

62.reading: For people of no learning to provoke the great, who excel in every respect, is, the verse tells a woman with full bangles, like hiding behind an erukku bush and driving an elephant to charge.
62.nuance: கைப்பித்தல், to make bitter, names the offence as needling rather than open attack, and the proverb answers it: the provoker thinks himself covered, but the erukku is a thin shrub no elephant notices. The verse sets the unlearned against the great, so the greatness here is chiefly of learning (எல்லாத் திறத்தும்). சொல்வின் in line 2 is read as சொல்லின்.

pazhamozhi.literal: hiding behind an erukku shrub and setting an elephant charging

story.act: no story; one who goads an elephant from behind a flimsy shrub that will not hide him

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the unlearned who needle the great trust a cover that cannot save them

63.reading: The verse asks, of the lord of a watered town where bees hum like a sweet-toned yaazh, whether anyone will bear with a man who has erred once before and errs again, greatly; does a plantain bear a bunch twice?
63.nuance: The question form expects 'no': forbearance is spent on the first offence. The proverb is apt because the plantain bears its one bunch and is cut down, so the second offence finds nothing left to give. The subject of பொறுப்பவோ is unstated; under the heading it is the great.

pazhamozhi.literal: does the plantain put out a bunch twice?

story.act: no story; the plantain that fruits once and is spent

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the great forgive a fault once, not a repeated one

64.reading: When the great see that those who have long been with them have left the right way, they tremble and are greatly pained, says the verse to the lord of a shore grove decked with adumbu creepers; the house of one who acts crookedly will perish.
64.nuance: நெடுங்காலம் வந்தார் makes the offenders long-standing dependents or associates, not strangers, and the great respond with dread and grief rather than anger; the ruin in the proverb follows the crooked man's own conduct. நலிவார் can also be transitive, 'they will greatly afflict them', which would make the great the agents of the ruin; the reading cannot be fixed.

pazhamozhi.literal: the house of one given to crooked conduct will surely perish

story.act: no story; the proverb names a type, the man of crooked ways and his family line

pazhamozhi.applied_to: long association with the great does not save one who strays from their way

links.note: Kural 891 ranks not slighting those able to act as the highest safeguard; Pazhamozhi 60 says calling the great small is neither wisdom, grace nor knowing, and brings harm.
links.teaches: The Kural values the restraint as self-protection; Pazhamozhi adds that the slight is also a failure of understanding, so the man who belittles the great is both unsafe and wrong about them.
links.list_adds: its threefold denial (not wisdom, not grace, not knowing) strips the slight of every merit before naming its harm, and the proverb says the slighted greatness itself survives.

links.note: Both use a damaged great building that keeps its function: Naladiyar 147's decayed house still has a dry corner, Pazhamozhi 60's assembly hall stays a hall when cut into. The reading of 60's proverb is uncertain.
links.teaches: The same image works from two sides: the Naladiyar uses it for what the well-born still do in hardship, Pazhamozhi for how others must still regard the great when their standing is damaged.
links.list_adds: it turns the quatrain's image of the well-born man's own constancy into a warning to those who would belittle him.

links.note: Kural 893 says, in grim irony, that one who wants ruin should offend the able; Pazhamozhi 61 has the small man offend the great because his senses are dazed and he cannot see his death.
links.teaches: The Kural frames offending the great as a choice of ruin, Pazhamozhi as blindness: held together they show the offence as willed in form and unseen in fact, the offender choosing what he cannot see.
links.list_adds: its proverb replaces the couplet's mock instruction with the dazed traveller, making the offender's fault a failure of sight rather than of will.

links.note: Naladiyar 64 says the excellent do not flare up when the low confront them with unfit words; Pazhamozhi 61 says the small who confront the great with insolence walk to their death.
links.teaches: The pair separates the great man's calm from the offender's fate: the great may not burn with anger, yet the insolent small man is lost all the same, so his safety never rested on their temper.
links.list_adds: it moves the scene from the great man's response to the offender's end, with the proverb's dazed traveller as the measure of his danger.

links.note: Kural 894 likens the weak doing harm to the strong to beckoning Death by hand; Pazhamozhi 62 likens the unlearned provoking the great to goading an elephant from behind an erukku shrub.
links.teaches: The Kural's weak man calls his death openly; Pazhamozhi's thinks he is hidden, so the pair adds a second folly to the first: misjudging one's cover as well as one's strength.
links.list_adds: the proverb adds the false shelter, the thin erukku, which the couplet's open gesture lacks, and names the provokers as the unlearned.

links.note: Naladiyar 164: a snake in a rock crevice still dreads thunder, and those who anger the great are not safe in a fortress; Pazhamozhi 62: the provoker hides behind an erukku shrub and goads an elephant.
links.teaches: Set side by side, the two hiding places run from the strongest to the weakest, a rock crevice and a fortress against a shrub, and both fail, so no shelter of any strength protects against the great.
links.list_adds: its proverb makes the shelter absurdly thin and the offender the one who starts the charge, where the quatrain's snake only fears.

links.note: Kural 152 says to bear with excess always (என்றும்) and better to forget it; Pazhamozhi 63 asks whether a man who errs again after a first fault will be borne, and answers with the plantain that bears once.
links.teaches: Against the Kural's 'always', Pazhamozhi sets a count: forbearance covers the first offence, and the repeated one is outside it, so the pair raises whether forbearance is unlimited or once given.
links.list_adds: the plantain proverb puts a number on forbearance, one bunch and no second, where the couplet sets no limit.

links.note: Naladiyar 161 warns not to offend even the faultless counting on their forgiveness, since once they turn away no one can undo it; Pazhamozhi 63 says a second offence after a first is not borne.
links.teaches: The quatrain warns against trading on forgiveness at all; Pazhamozhi shows when the trade fails, at the second offence, so together they mark forgiveness as real but single.
links.list_adds: it fixes the point at which the quatrain's turning away comes, the repetition, through the plantain that fruits once.

links.note: Kural 898 says those who seem to stand forever vanish with their line (குடியொடு) when the hill-like are slighted; Pazhamozhi 64 says the house (குடி) of the crooked perishes while the great only tremble and grieve.
links.teaches: Both make the offender's line the casualty, but Pazhamozhi has the great grieve rather than strike, so the ruin of the family comes from the offence itself and not from the great man's wrath.
links.list_adds: it makes the offenders the great man's own long-standing people and gives the great dread and grief, where the couplet gives them only height.

links.note: Kural 806 says those who keep bounds do not give up an old bond even when ruin comes; Pazhamozhi 64 has the great keep feeling for long-standing associates who go astray, yet their house perishes.
links.teaches: The pair shows the limit of old loyalty: the great do not cast the old associate off, they grieve for him, but their constancy cannot stop the ruin his crooked conduct brings.
links.list_adds: it sets the loyal great man's grief beside the old associate's ruin, so the couplet's constancy is shown to be powerless to save.

links.note: Both have the small or unlearned offend the great and end in an image of unseen danger: 61 a dazed man who does not see his death, 62 a man who thinks an erukku shrub hides him from an elephant.
links.teaches: Read together, the two proverbs name the two blindnesses of the offender: he does not see the danger at all, or he sees it and wrongly trusts a cover.

source_issues: 60: Line 4 என்றூடு is obscure; the proverb's sense cannot be fixed.
61: Only a closing quotation mark is printed after வாறு; the opening mark is missing, so the proverb's start is not marked.
62: சொல்வின் in line 2 is probably சொல்லின்.
